article_title: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement
citation: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement. (2017). Chapter 7 of Teaching in Context: The Social Side of Education Reform, Harvard Education Press. https://www.harvardeducationpress.com
title: Improve schools by creating conditions and structures that let teachers share knowledge and work together effectively
description: The chapter's parent book proposes an alternative to individual-focused teacher quality enhancement: "creating conditions and school structures that facilitate the transmission and sharing of knowledge among teachers, allowing teachers to work together effectively." It rests on evidence that teachers become more effective when organizations support them in comprehensive and coordinated ways, capitalizing on what is known about how educators learn and improve.
requirements: School organizations must support teachers in comprehensive and coordinated ways
target_learners: teachers
school leaders
target_learning_goals: teacher improvement through knowledge transmission and collaborative work
examples: The book's studies feature leading scholars showing teachers become more effective in organizations that support them comprehensively and in coordinated ways.
key_sources: How the Organization of Schools and Local Communities Shape Educational Improvement. (2017). Chapter 7 of Teaching in Context: The Social Side of Education Reform, Harvard Education Press. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/how-organization-schools-and-local-communities-shape-educational-improvement

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Oregon parent assessment-literacy modules
description: Oregon's Department of Education, working with Behavioral Research & Teaching at the University of Oregon and other partners, "created five modules on topics such as the purpose of statewide assessments, how to make sense of assessment results, and how to support learning at home." Each module includes a fact sheet and video in both English and Spanish and lets users listen in on a conversation between a teacher and a parent or guardian. The brief presents the modules as a promising state strategy for increasing parents' assessment literacy.
requirements: Modules were customized to align with state and district assessment data in comparable efforts, suggesting alignment with local assessment systems is needed
target_learners: parents and guardians of K-12 students in Oregon
target_learning_goals: understanding the purpose of statewide assessments, interpreting results, and supporting learning at home
examples: Each module includes a fact sheet and video in English and Spanish featuring a simulated teacher-parent conversation
key_sources: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658190

article_title: Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose
citation: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed.
title: Oracle and tutor metaphors: how students' figurative framings of LLMs shape expectations that exceed the systems' pedagogical and epistemic capabilities
description: The chapter analyzes the two most prevalent student metaphors for LLMs: an oracle, conveying swift authoritative access to information, and a tutor, conveying personalized pedagogical support. Metaphors act as "cognitive scaffolding that helps people navigate and interpret unfamiliar tools" while also shaping uptake. The author argues the tutor metaphor "risks overstating the reliability of LLMs and wrongly imbues them with pedagogical intentionality," since LLMs do not track understanding or scaffold misconceptions, encouraging trust precisely where students' ability to evaluate accuracy is weakest.
requirements: Metaphor analysis draws on questionnaire responses in which students themselves articulated the metaphors and their associated hopes and worries
constraints: Analysis is based on a single 100-respondent questionnaire plus literature, not generalizable on its own per the author
target_learners: higher-education students, predominantly engineering
target_learning_goals: critical understanding of what LLMs are and are not
epistemic vigilance in AI-supported learning
examples: Students described LLMs as an expert truth-teller for search and synthesis, and as a low-barrier individual explainer, while simultaneously reporting hallucinations and verification burdens
key_sources: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16626

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Oral defence and dialogic accountability as integrity artefacts evaluating understanding rather than artefacts
description: Oral defence practices provide a dialogic mechanism through which learners articulate and justify academic decision-making in GenAI-augmented work, with prompts about where and how GenAI supported the work and which outputs were rejected or revised and why. The paper argues that "responsiveness to probing questions, conceptual grasp of disciplinary ideas, and the ability to articulate boundaries of appropriateness provide more robust indicators of learning and responsibility than similarity metrics or probabilistic detection tools."
requirements: Clear criteria, shared calibration among instructors, and flexibility in modality are essential; evaluative criteria must prioritize conceptual understanding rather than rhetorical fluency alone
constraints: In larger classes, formats may need adaptation through brief structured conferences, small-group dialogic checks, or selective sampling
target_learners: higher education students, including those with diverse language backgrounds
target_learning_goals: ownership of meaning, limitations, and disciplinary implications of GenAI-augmented work
examples: Typical prompts ask where and how GenAI supported the work, or how the final product might be adapted for a specific learner, context, or disciplinary constraint
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Orchestrate GenAI feedback with student feedback literacy for positive alignment
description: The paper's central design principle is that GenAI becomes an enabler of feedback engagement only when orchestrated with what students bring, especially their feedback literacy. A mismatch between an individual's feedback literacy and the GenAI environment's affordances 'could lessen the enabling role of GenAI in feedback engagement', so the challenge is 'constructing synergies between individual students' feedback literacy and the GenAI feedback environment'.
requirements: Students must develop feedback literacy capacities suited to the GenAI context, including prompt writing, evaluative judgement and ethical awareness
constraints: GenAI's affordances do not necessarily lead to in-depth student feedback engagement without this alignment
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: deep engagement with feedback for learning improvement
examples: Student B's high feedback literacy enabled deep engagement with ChatGPT feedback, while Student A's low literacy led to superficial copying of revisions
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future
citation: Fenton, A. (2025). Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future. Educational Researcher, 54(7), 430-436. https://doi.org/10.3102/0013189X251333638
title: Implement oral assessments with clear guidelines, rubrics, question banks, and student-facing support to reduce anxiety and protect fairness
description: The article's practical recommendations hold that oral assessments work well only when carefully prepared: students "should be given information about the schedule and assessment criteria beforehand and have some experience of the format," assessments should use a clear mastery-level rubric with a bank of questions linked to learning objectives, and educators should provide student-facing support such as recorded mock assessments and no-stakes practice to reduce anxiety, particularly for high school and undergraduate students.
requirements: Clear guidelines for staff and students, examiner training or shadowing with experienced instructors, identity verification, a calibration process for larger cohorts, and clear prompting rules
constraints: Careful attention to fairness, validity, and reliability is required; oral assessments should not be the only means of examination and content should be standardized as much as possible
target_learners: high school students
undergraduate students
online or distance learning students
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of knowledge and application
reduced test anxiety
academic integrity
examples: The article recommends an oral assessment take no more than 20 minutes to get a clear picture of a student's understanding, planning for half as many harder problems (Sayre, 2014), and using shared online spreadsheets for scheduling to reduce administrative effort
key_sources: Fenton, A. (2025). Reconsidering the Use of Oral Exams and Assessments: An Old Way to Move Into a New Future. Educational Researcher, 54(7), 430-436. https://doi.org/10.3102/0013189X251333638

article_title: Oral corrective feedback in second language classrooms
citation: Roy Lyster, Kazuya Saito, and Masatoshi Sato. (2013). Oral corrective feedback in second language classrooms. Language Teaching, Volume 46, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261444812000365
title: Taxonomy of oral corrective feedback types in L2 classrooms
description: The review's organizing taxonomy identifies the various types of oral corrective feedback teachers provide in second language classrooms. As the abstract states, "Various types of oral CF are first identified", establishing a classification of CF moves (such as recasts, prompts, and explicit correction, as discussed in the review) that structures the subsequent synthesis of frequency, preference, and effectiveness research. This taxonomy serves as the framework through which the review compares CF across instructional contexts and studies.
requirements: The taxonomy requires distinguishing CF moves by their characteristics, such as explicitness and whether they push learners to repair their own output
constraints: The taxonomy is developed for oral corrective feedback in second language classroom settings
target_learners: Second language learners in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Second language linguistic accuracy and development

article_title: Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis
citation: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll
title: Organizational perspective on teacher turnover and school staffing problems
description: Drawn from the sociology of organizations, occupations, and work, this framework holds that teacher turnover and staffing problems cannot be fully understood without examining employing organizations. It rests on three premises: "understanding employee turnover is important because of its link to the performance and effectiveness of organizations"; turnover must be examined "at the level of the organization"; and turnover requires examining "the character and conditions of the organizations within which employees work." From this view, migration matters as much as attrition, and high turnover is both outcome and cause of school dysfunction.
requirements: Analysis must examine turnover at the organizational level, treating both migration and attrition as relevant departures
constraints: The article states it does not attempt a comprehensive analysis of all aspects of school organization that may affect turnover, focusing on four policy-amenable conditions
target_learners: School administrators and policymakers concerned with teacher retention
target_learning_goals: Understanding and reducing school staffing problems through improved teacher retention
examples: The study applied the framework to SASS/TFS data, testing four organizational conditions—compensation, administrative support, conflict, and faculty influence—across a range of schools and turnover subsets.

article_title: Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? A Review of Studies into the Relationship Between Oral Communicative Competence and Sociometric Status in Childhood
citation: Femke van der Wilt, Chiel van der Veen, Claudia van Kruistum, Bert van Oers (2019). Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? A Review of Studies into the Relationship Between Oral Communicative Competence and Sociometric Status in Childhood. Educational Psychology Review (2019) 31:699–724. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09479-z
title: Oral communicative competence as a context-dependent, multifaceted construct
description: The review defines oral communicative competence, following Hymes, as the ability to convey and interpret messages and negotiate meanings interpersonally within specific social contexts. It is "a context-dependent and multifaceted construct that consists of many sub-abilities that need to be integrated to communicate effectively", encompassing socio-linguistic competence alongside structural knowledge of language. The review uses this construct to organize its search terms, its inclusion criteria, and its analysis of how studies operationalize children's communication.
requirements: Assessment should take the interactional context into account, since appropriateness of language use depends on settings, topics, and relationships among people
constraints: The construct is broad and multifaceted, which makes it difficult to define and operationalize; standardized tests may not capture its full complexity
target_learners: children aged 1 to 12 years in mainstream community samples
target_learning_goals: oral communicative competence: using language acceptably and efficiently in particular social contexts

article_title: The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension∗
citation: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555
title: Visual marking of oral phrase boundaries facilitates children's reading comprehension
description: The article proposes that children comprehend oral discourse better than written discourse because speech supplies "the added underlying structural cues available when the English language is spoken". Written punctuation marks major clauses but not finer boundaries, so the two segmentation formats were designed to present "a visual analogue of the underlying grammatical and structural constituents found in oral discourse". The results lend support to this theory, though the author notes it was not conclusively supported because oral discourse was never directly compared with the segmented written formats.
requirements: The segmentation must mark phrase boundaries without changing the words or punctuation of the text
constraints: The study did not directly compare oral discourse with the segmented written formats, so the theory has not been conclusively supported
target_learners: elementary school children in grades 4 and 7
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of written discourse at or above grade level
examples: The pausal phrase format placed phrases on individual lines (mean 5.8 words) at points where 50% of an adult sample would pause reading aloud; the syntactic phrase format separated noun phrases, verb phrases, and pattern completers (mean three words per line)
key_sources: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555

article_title: Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics
citation: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462
title: Orientation discrimination task as a measure of children's visual processing
description: An adaptive psychophysical task used to assess visual processing in young children. Children judge whether a second bicolor segment turned clockwise or anticlockwise relative to a first segment; a three-down-one-up staircase (step size 1.0715°, starting from 10.239°) converges on the orientation discrimination threshold, computed as the mean angle difference over the middle six of ten reversals per block. The article notes "The lower the threshold, the higher the visual processing ability." Children sat 80 cm from the screen, and bicolor segments replaced pure lines to ease task demands for children.
requirements: Children must understand the representation of the segment and the spatial relations between the two segments
Bicolor segments were introduced after piloting because pure lines and dots were too difficult for children
constraints: The authors note this task "is only one kind of visual discrimination" and call for future studies to include other visual processing components such as shape, color, and size
target_learners: Kindergarten and early primary school children
target_learning_goals: Assessment of visual processing as a precursor skill for reading and mathematics
examples: Used at senior kindergarten in a longitudinal study of 82 mainland Chinese children, with reliability 0.79 (Table 1)
key_sources: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462

article_title: Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults
citation: Blackburne LK, Eddy MD, Kalra P, Yee D, Sinha P, Gabrieli JDE. (2014) Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults. PLoS ONE 9(5): e98386. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098386
title: Orientation-insensitive object recognition account of letter reversal development
description: The article advances the explanatory account that learning to read adapts general object recognition processes that are insensitive to right-left orientation. As the authors put it, "learning to read reflects a specialized adaptation of more general object recognition processes that are insensitive to right-left orientation", so reading experience is needed to overcome this initial orientation insensitivity and establish orientation-specific letter representations. The study's finding that children up to age 12 show no early ERP or fMRI distinction between typical and reversed letters, while adults do, is interpreted as evidence that this specialized, orientation-specific letter perception develops slowly.
requirements: Reading experience over a prolonged developmental period to establish orientation-specific letter representations
constraints: The article states the developmental process remains immature at least through age 12 even in above-average readers; the account is offered as an interpretation of the observed neural differences, not as a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: Children ages 5–12 learning to read
Beginning readers
target_learning_goals: Orientation-specific letter perception and recognition of letters such as b/d and p/q
examples: Children ages 5–12 viewing typical and reversed letters showed no P1 or N170 ERP differences and little fMRI difference, whereas adults showed large differences in the same tasks
key_sources: Blackburne LK, Eddy MD, Kalra P, Yee D, Sinha P, Gabrieli JDE. (2014) Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults. PLoS ONE 9(5): e98386. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098386

article_title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: Deconstructed facets of orchestration load
description: The article treats orchestration load not as a black box but as a multifaceted notion encompassing content load (e.g. evaluating multiple student answers), cognitive load (processing new information in short activities), and the effort of diagnosing deviations and using orchestration technology. It models teachers' actionable differences under different support provisions to derive these facets, arguing "all types of load, i.e., content, orchestration and cognitive load, reflect the valuable and attentive cognitive processing teachers are required to engage in real-time". The load a provision adds or removes is read from how it changes teachers' orchestration actions.
requirements: Analysis of orchestration load requires modelling teachers' observable orchestration actions under contrasting support conditions
constraints: Existing definitions of orchestration load remain fuzzy, with different definitions across the literature the article cites; no standard measurements to quantify orchestration load are available
target_learners: teachers orchestrating CSCL activities in co-located classrooms
target_learning_goals: effective real-time regulation of scripted collaborative learning
examples: Six teachers' orchestration actions were modelled with ENA under no-dashboard, mirroring, and guiding conditions to derive load facets
key_sources: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9

article_title: Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities
citation: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623
title: Select and orchestrate instructional strategies based on contextual factors rather than declaring one method superior
description: The article's central position is that "adequate instruction always involves different strategies, which should be thoughtfully selected based on contextual factors." Most real learning environments mix telling students things with opportunities to explore and invent; the key difference between methods is whether full explanation precedes investigation or students generate part of the content themselves. Designers and teachers should therefore orchestrate both approaches depending on topic, goal, student, teacher, and design.
requirements: Teachers need thorough training in the theoretical background of inquiry-based learning and its classroom implementation.
constraints: The distinction between direct instruction and guided inquiry is not always straightforward because student activity plays a role in both.
target_learners: Science students from elementary through secondary education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of science domains
examples: The article notes Open Science curricula and project-based programs contain "a rich mixture of telling students certain things and having them figure out other things."

article_title: Teachers’ Feedback on Oral Reading: A Critical Review of its Effects and the use of Theory in Research
citation: Grønli, K. M., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E. M., & Uppstad, P. H. (2024). Teachers' Feedback on Oral Reading: A Critical Review of its Effects and the use of Theory in Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09957-z
title: Eleven-component taxonomy of teacher feedback during oral reading, organized into four main feedback types
description: The review codes the feedback practices in 24 K–5 oral-reading studies into a taxonomy of feedback content. It reports: "We identified 11 components of feedback content in the various feedback practices reviewed. These components fall into four main types of feedback: performance feedback, supporting elements, explicit corrective feedback, and implicit feedback encouraging independent thinking about their reading". The components range from reading-rate and error information through goals and rewards to word-reading, comprehension, and prosody instruction and questions as feedback.
requirements: Feedback practices in primary studies must be codable into the 11 content components, with combined practices treated as single practices with measured effects
constraints: Visual elements appeared in several studies but their effects were not uniquely measured and were not further analyzed
target_learners: K–5 students (age 5–11) in school-based reading instruction
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency
Reading comprehension
Reading motivation
examples: The review's bubble chart (Table 1) maps the frequency of studies across the 11 feedback types and their examined effects on fluency, comprehension, and motivation

description: The answer key and score sheet for Form B prints standard scores by grade: 18 for grade 3, 26 for grade 4, 33 for grade 5, 38 for grade 6, 42 for grade 7, 47 for grade 8, and 52 for grade 9. The key also lists acceptable number sequences for each exercise and the point value attached to each correct answer, allowing cumulative scoring against the grade norms.

constraints: Standard scores are printed only for Form B in the material presented

article_title: Unpacking the unique relationship between set for variability and word reading development: Examining word- and child-level predictors of performance.
citation: Edwards, A. A., Steacy, L. M., Seigelman, N., Rigobon, V. M., Kearns, D. M., Rueckl, J. G., & Compton, D. L. (2022). Unpacking the Unique Relationship Between Set for Variability and Word Reading Development: Examining Word- and Child-Level Predictors of Performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000696
title: Orthographic facilitation account of Set for Variability: a phonological clean-up process augmented by phonology-to-orthography knowledge
description: The article proposes that the SfV task taps a phonologically-based "clean-up" process, analogous to phonological cleanup units in connectionist reading models, that allows children to disambiguate the mismatch between a decoded form and the actual lexical pronunciation. It further hypothesizes orthographic facilitation: children may use phonology-to-orthography associations to translate a mispronounced spoken word into an orthographic form and access the correct phonological form, a process rooted in the orthographic skeleton hypothesis. The account predicts facilitation only for children with sufficient decoding skill and for items with greater phonology-orthography consistency.
requirements: Children need sufficient decoding skill to activate phonology-to-orthography connections during the task
constraints: The article states those with low word attack skills are essentially unaffected by phonology-orthography consistency regardless of word identification skill
Word attack is described as not a pure indicator of phonology-to-orthography connection knowledge
target_learners: Children in grades 2–5 learning to read English
target_learning_goals: Disambiguating decoded forms of irregular words to reach correct lexical pronunciations
Word reading development
examples: The study modeled item-level SfV responses of 489 grade 2–5 children with hierarchical cross-classified models including phonology-only and phonology-orthography predictors

article_title: Parallel and serial reading processes in children’s word and nonword reading.
citation: van den Boer, M., & de Jong, P. F. (2015). Parallel and serial reading processes in children's word and nonword reading. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(1), 141-151. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037101
title: Debate on the representation of orthographic knowledge: word-specific lexicon versus sublexical associative network
description: The article organizes its inquiry around an unresolved question in reading research: whether fluent word identification relies on orthographic knowledge that is "an accumulation of word-specific knowledge in a lexicon acquired through decoding or as a well-developed associative network of sublexical units". The authors test which account fits by examining whether word and nonword reading are underlain by serial or parallel processing, using digit naming tasks as process markers.
requirements: Distinguishing serial from parallel processing requires correlation patterns of string reading with both serial and discrete digit naming tasks
constraints: The article reports its own results are "not fully in line" with either current theoretical position
target_learners: children in grades 2, 3, and 5 learning to read
target_learning_goals: fluent and accurate word identification (reading development)
examples: The authors administered digit, word, and nonword naming tasks to 314 Dutch children and used latent class analyses to infer each reader's processing mode
key_sources: van den Boer, M., & de Jong, P. F. (2015). Parallel and serial reading processes in children's word and nonword reading. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(1), 141-151. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037101

article_title: The reading comprehension and vocabulary knowledge of children with poor reading comprehension despite adequate decoding: Evidence from a regression-based matching approach.
citation: Spencer, M., Wagner, R. K., & Petscher, Y. (2019). The Reading Comprehension and Vocabulary Knowledge of Children with Poor Reading Comprehension despite Adequate Decoding: Evidence from a Regression-Based Matching Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000274
title: Add oral language measures such as receptive vocabulary to early assessment batteries to identify children who struggle to comprehend text
description: Because word-reading skills appear relatively intact in children with SCD, common at-risk screens miss them. The article recommends that "measures of oral language, such as vocabulary, may be a useful addition to assessment batteries that are used to identify children who struggle to comprehend text." Receptive vocabulary can be assessed as early as age 3, enabling identification before children are already failing to comprehend in second or third grade.
requirements: Oral language screening measures should be comprehensive, including measures beyond only receptive vocabulary, since vocabulary development is influenced by numerous factors
constraints: Reading comprehension itself is unlikely to be assessed reliably prior to formal schooling
target_learners: preschool and early elementary children (from age 3 through early grades)
target_learning_goals: early identification of reading comprehension difficulties
examples: The study used the PPVT receptive vocabulary measure alongside decoding and comprehension measures to characterize SCD children's oral language weakness across five cohorts.

article_title: Reading ability conflates SES creativity gaps
citation: Guilherme Lichand, Lêticia Lopes, Sachin Allums. (2026). Reading ability conflates SES creativity gaps. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00404-y
title: Assessments of higher-order skills should account for limitations in foundational skills, e.g., by administering oral exams or non-verbal measures
description: The article recommends that creativity and other higher-order-skill assessments better account for limitations in foundational skills such as reading, which are disproportionately concentrated among low-income students. Concretely, it suggests that "assessors might consider administering oral exams or even non-verbal measures of creativity or other higher-order skills in order to accurately capture underlying skills." This follows from the experimental finding that removing reading requirements eliminates or reverses SES gaps. The authors also warn that unfair test design "might end up reinforcing deficit narratives that mischaracterize the potential of disadvantaged students."
requirements: Assessment items must otherwise be answerable verbally or non-verbally, as in the trials where students responded aloud and enumerators recorded responses
constraints: The article notes it remains unclear whether the findings extend to convergent thinking, form-first vs function-first divergent tasks, or figural creativity; reading instructions aloud in figural tasks might help but this cannot be said for certain
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly low-SES students with limited reading proficiency
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of creative thinking and other higher-order skills
examples: In Studies 2 and 3, enumerators read question prompts aloud in the treatment condition and typed students' spoken answers in both conditions, isolating creativity from reading and writing ability

article_title: Jim Greer’s and Mary Mark’s Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals
citation: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z
title: Orchestration systems fall into three broad types and bring new teacher-focused evaluable goals
description: The article argues that the centrality of the human teacher in classrooms using AIED systems has led to "orchestration" systems (Dillenbourg 2013) that assist teachers to manage the added complexity. "These orchestration systems fall into three broad types": systems for classes where all learners work with an AIED system and the teacher needs help targeting extra help; systems helping teachers track learners using more standard technology; and systems working directly with learners while offering the teacher a dashboard of general difficulties. They open new evaluable goals, e.g. "the degree to which the human teacher's time is being used effectively", changes in the division of labour, better diagnosis of difficulties, and reification of orchestration for teacher reflection.
requirements: Such systems assume a human teacher in the loop, with learners exposed to individual or small-group work with the AIED system, interaction with the teacher, and whole-class teaching
constraints: Orchestration systems were not yet built when Mark and Greer (1993) wrote, and were not strongly in evidence at Greer's 2016 retrospective
target_learners: school students in classes where the teacher deploys AIED systems
target_learning_goals: effective use of scarce teacher time
teacher awareness of learner difficulties
teacher reflection on planned versus actual orchestration
examples: ASSISTments is described as a system students use for homework which "also provides, the next day, an analysis for the teacher of their common and individual difficulties to help the teacher choose what issues to focus on."

article_title: The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology
citation: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9
title: Two-dimension framework of quality theoretical scholarship: originality and utility
description: The editorial adopts Corley and Gioia's framework for judging theoretical contributions in borrower disciplines. It states that "The authors delineated two key dimensions of quality theoretical scholarship: originality and utility." Originality means contributing new ideas through original synthesis, applications to practice, methodological development, or wholly new conceptual understandings about teaching and learning. Utility means theory matters "to the degree that it is useful and can have an actual impact on the world". The editorial applies this framework to learning design and technology, a field that likewise borrows from many disciplines and speaks to both academics and practitioners.
requirements: Theoretical work must contribute new ideas to the academic discourse, per the originality dimension
constraints: The framework was synthesized for business management, a field the editorial says similarly self-identifies as a borrower discipline
target_learners: education researchers and journal reviewers in learning design and technology
target_learning_goals: evaluating the quality of theoretical scholarship
examples: The editorial used this framework, together with Whetten's practical considerations, to inspire its special-issue review rubric

bracket positioning
psychomotor clinical skills

citation: Nail M. Alhajya, Sumaia S. Alzaghamim, Yousef M. Arouri. (2018). THE IMPACT OF VIRTUAL TRIPS ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF ARABIC LANGUAGE ORAL SKILLS AMONG THIRD GRADE STUDENTS IN JORDAN. Journal of Technology and Science Education, 8(1), 72-85. https://doi.org/10.3926/jotse.331
title: Al-Hallaq's four-section taxonomy of oral skills
description: The article presents a four-part organization of oral skills drawn from Al-Hallaq (2010): understanding skills and their accuracy (willingness to listen, concentration, following oral instructions), comprehension skills (summarizing the audible, distinguishing truth from fiction, recognizing and classifying relationships between ideas), remembering skills (recognizing new audio, linking new learning with past experience, choosing ideas to keep in memory), and literary tasting and critical thinking skills (engaging with the speaker emotionally, judging strengths and weaknesses, and predicting how the conversation will end). The article uses this framework to argue that oral skills are a prerequisite for reading, writing, and other language skills.

article_title: Polyrhythmic Tapping: Examining the Effectiveness of the Strategy of Organizing Rhythmic Structures through Synthesis
citation: Hamit Yokus, Tuba Yokus. (2015). Polyrhythmic Tapping: Examining the Effectiveness of the Strategy of Organizing Rhythmic Structures through Synthesis. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.1.1917
title: Strategy of organizing rhythmic structures through synthesis
description: A cognitive strategy the authors name and define for performing difficult polyrhythms that "cannot be divided into equal durations" in standard notation. It has eight operational phases: calculating the least common denominator, determining the units, matching units with suitable notations, classifying note forms, arranging grouped units according to the meter's main beat, identifying the relationship between the original and new structure, doing mental pre-rhythmic synthesizing, and applying the rhythm using the integrated hierarchical approach. Mental pre-rhythmic synthesizing provides preliminary mental preparation, with the rhythm counted in the mind during performance.
requirements: A two-hour training session teaching the strategy, followed by a week of independent practice with a metronome, as used in the study
constraints: The article positions it as an alternative strategy for difficult polyrhythmic structures that require advanced education to play or tap
target_learners: undergraduate music education students
target_learning_goals: performing 3:2, 4:3, 8:3, 5:4 and 3:5 polyrhythmic structures
examples: The experimental group was taught the strategy via direct instruction in a two-hour session, practiced with a metronome for a week, then significantly outperformed controls on the Polyrhythmic Tapping Test

description: The Oracy Skills Framework, developed by the University of Cambridge team, sets out the oracy skills students need for learning and life. It is intended to be relevant in any context, formal or informal, within and beyond school, and underpins the design of the dedicated Year 7 curriculum, oracy in every lesson, and the Oracy Assessment Toolkit.

article_title: Oracy Curriculum, Culture and Assessment Toolkit: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Maxwell, B., Burnett, C., Reidy, J., Willis, B., & Demack, S. (2015). Oracy Curriculum, Culture and Assessment Toolkit: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Oracy Assessment Toolkit: three pre/post assessment tasks, six assessment-for-learning tasks, and a rating scheme
description: The Oracy Assessment Toolkit measures the skills set out in the Oracy Skills Framework. It includes three assessment tasks for beginning and end of Year 7: "a formal presentational speech; an instructional activity whereby one student enables another to complete a specific task; and a group discussion in which three students are asked to reach joint conclusions about a specific topic". A rating scheme lets teachers rate each relevant framework skill, build a skills profile per student, and track progress across the year. Six additional assessment-for-learning tasks can be used flexibly and adapted to a school's existing curriculum.
requirements: Should be used following training to enhance the reliability of the tool
constraints: The assessment tool was under development between pre and post test, sample sizes in the pilot were small, and it is not yet a standardised assessment test

examples: Exemplar videos of assessment grading were made available on the University of Cambridge website to enable teachers to moderate their grading.

title: OrCheTaboo game (Taboo-adapted card game for organic chemistry functional groups)

citation: Popov V, Rochlen LR. (2025). From communication to action: using ordered network analysis to model team performance in clinical simulation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07062-5
title: Ordered network analysis (ONA) as a method for modeling team communication sequences as dynamic networks
description: ONA is a network-modeling methodology that takes coded interaction data as input and models sequences of coded behaviors as networks. The article states that "ONA models sequences of coded behaviors as networks, quantitatively identifying the frequency of speech acts, order, and temporal connections between them." Using a moving stanza window and singular value decomposition, it represents each team's communication pattern as a point in a metric space, enabling statistical and visual comparison of networks between groups (e.g., high- vs low-performing teams). In this study ONA was applied to TuRBO-coded simulation dialogue with a 4-line moving stanza window.
requirements: Requires coded data (e.g., TuRBO-annotated transcripts), specification of units of analysis, conversations, moving stanza window size, and codes; the article used a 4-line window because team members took on average 4 sentences to exchange information on the same topic.
constraints: The authors state that identified patterns "cannot be generalized to similar real-world clinical situations without extensive additional analysis of the fidelity of the simulation scenario."

target_learning_goals: team communication and coordination during crisis management
transition from situation assessment to planning and implementation
examples: The study transcribed and segmented 22 simulation videos in ELAN, coded them with the TuRBO framework (Cohen's kappa = 0.73), and applied the ONA R package to compare high- and low-performing teams' networks.

description: A theoretical framework for implementing quality improvement in healthcare organisations, which structured this study's analysis. The NetworkZ team used OQ to design implementation activities and as the deductive coding framework for staff interviews, noting the challenges are interconnected and can work together synergistically in either direction.
requirements: Application requires coding data deductively against the original definitions of the six challenges, with researchers meeting regularly to discuss whether emerging findings fall within the framework.

title: Produce organized, relevant pre-class materials of manageable difficulty, using student perceptions as design clues
description: The article recommends that "significant attention should be paid to producing more organized and relevant pre-class materials based on established instructional rules and principles." Instructors should "first focus on the learning contents that students can handle rather than on what the instructors themselves desire to deliver," because some tutors condensed too much information into pre-class readings and lectures. Students' perceptions of the consistency and difficulty of pre-class materials may provide clues concerning likely learning outcomes, and better tutor training for the new method is implied as a need.

Adherence to instructional design rules and principles when producing materials

target_learning_goals: comprehension of pre-class lecture and reading content
preparedness for in-class problem solving

title: Organisational justice theory as the framework for applicant perceptions of selection procedures
description: The article adopts organisational justice theory as "The dominant theoretical framework on applicant perceptions". It distinguishes distributive justice, the fairness of outcome distribution, from procedural justice, the fairness of allocation procedures. Within Gilliland's model of applicant reactions, procedural justice perceptions are shaped by formal characteristics of the selection system such as job relatedness and opportunity to perform, which the study used to test SJT design features.
requirements: The framework requires measuring applicant perceptions of formal characteristics of the selection system, such as face validity, applicant differentiation, study relatedness and chance to perform.
constraints: The article notes perceptions of procedural justice are also determined by treatment of applicants and explanations of procedures (interactional justice), beyond the formal characteristics studied here.
target_learners: medical school applicants
target_learning_goals: fair and acceptable admission selection procedures
examples: The study measured four procedural justice formal-characteristic items and ease of cheating for eleven admission instruments, using the formal characteristics component to test SJT design features.

title: Skill-deficit account of inadequate plaque removal despite daily brushing
description: The article proposes that high prevalence of gingivitis despite reported daily hygiene "indicates a lack of oral hygiene skills". From the movement-sciences perspective it adopts, skill training requires many repetitions of the same movements to incorporate them into the motor program, a prerequisite for automation of skills. Computer-based training is presented as a means to deliver these repetitions in small steps with standardization, repeatability, and transparency.
requirements: many repetitions of the same movements in very small steps to automate the skill
constraints: the article notes prior comparison studies suffered from lack of control groups, non-blinded examiners, or missing standardization
target_learners: adults performing daily oral hygiene
target_learning_goals: improved oral hygiene skills and gingival health
examples: A representative German sample: more than 30% responded negatively when asked whether they knew any brushing technique

article_title: Reinforcing outpatient medical student learning using brief computer tutorials: the Patient-Teacher-Tutorial sequence.
citation: Pusic Martin V, MacDonald Wendy A, Eisman Harley O, Black John B. (2012). Reinforcing outpatient medical student learning using brief computer tutorials: the Patient-Teacher-Tutorial sequence. BMC Medical Education, 12:70. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-70
title: Brief self-contained computer tutorials on Oral Rehydration Solutions and Fever Without Source
description: Two brief computer tutorials were designed for use by medical students in the Pediatric Emergency Department, presenting mainly declarative knowledge. The ORS tutorial (30 screens) targeted conceptual knowledge of osmosis and facilitated diffusion; the FWS tutorial (42 screens) targeted factual knowledge of the diagnostic and treatment approach to febrile children aged birth-36 months. Instructional strategies "included animations, schematic diagrams, interactive exercises and patient presentations but not video". They were installed on a single computer at the nursing station and were independently reviewed by content experts and pilot tested to saturation.
requirements: Installed on a computer located in the clinical area so the tutorial can be done immediately in the flow of patient care
constraints: The tutorials were invariant "black boxes" with fixed instructional strategies that may not have been optimal for a given student situation; they were not available to students outside the study
target_learners: third-year medical students on a Pediatric Emergency rotation
target_learning_goals: physiologic principles of oral rehydration
diagnostic and treatment approach to fever without source
examples: Students randomized to the in-sequence condition completed the tutorial matching the index patient they had just seen
